items.title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01
items.q: And in through Manuel, I went with King Oliver. And that was in 1927... But on trumpet there, they had King Oliver... On saxophone we had Omar Simeon.

ctx.x: In the cold weather when they played.

So, in the, up until, I went back with Solis there, last of 25 and I stayed until 27. And by that time King Oliver had heard that record, My Josephine and hearing all the work on the saxophone. And right down to Manuel Perez and found who it was and Manuel told him who it was. And in through Manuel, I went with King Oliver. And that was in 1927.
Where was he when he located you then? He was in Chicago.

items.title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01
items.q: The interviewer asks about Joe Oliver's playing ability ('How he was playing... What did you think of it?') and the interviewee responds ('He could play real well then.'), but the interviewee does not claim to have personally known, met, or worked with Joe Oliver in the provided text.

ctx.x: The Cajun country is what I meant to say, over that way.

D.D. heard him sing that and D.D. picked it up from him. Yeah. But D.D. didn't get the thing right, you see. Now I'm going to give you an idea how he'd go. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. That's where the Mayor of Pompon added. Yeah. But D.D. got it mixed up. D.D. came out. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. Yeah, he got it wrong and it just spread like that. So, well anyway, we had Nellie Lutcher, that was our piano player, and I can forget her father's name, he was our bass player, and a…
